definitions.definition: A piece of software that controls all the computer's resources and provides the base upon which application programs can be written.
An executive for embedded applications that meets task deadlines in addition to producing logically correct results.
A real-time system in which missing an individual deadline results in catastrophic failure and great financial loss, e.g. air traffic control, nuclear plant control.
A real-time system where a missed deadline causes an unacceptable quality reduction but the economic disaster risk is limited, e.g. automobile ignition failure.
A real-time system where a deadline may be missed and recovered from, with reduction in quality and performance kept at an acceptable level, e.g. multimedia transmission.
The time between executing the last instruction of an interrupted task and the first instruction of the interrupt handler; an RTOS requires it to be short and predictable.
The time taken while saving the context of the current task and then switching over to another task; it should be short in an RTOS.
Switching from a currently executing task to a higher-priority task that is ready and waiting to be executed.
A multi-user, multi-tasking, machine-independent operating system created by Kenneth Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at AT&T Bell Labs in 1969.
The hub of the UNIX operating system; it allocates time and memory to programs and handles the file store and communications in response to system calls.
A command line interpreter acting as the interface between user and kernel; it interprets commands typed by the user and arranges for them to be carried out.
Data structure in a UNIX-style file system storing all attributes of a file and identified by a unique number.
A UNIX facility that links commands together so the output of one program becomes the input of another program or command.
The length T of time between any two consecutive instants at which the inputs are sampled; a key design choice on which the digital controller's behaviour critically depends.
A system whose state variables, monitored by multiple sensors, have different dynamics and therefore require different sampling periods to achieve smooth response.
The variation in a job's response time from period to period; some control systems impose the requirement that it not exceed a threshold.
A set of data objects is absolutely temporally consistent if the maximum age of the objects in the set is no greater than a certain threshold.
A set of data objects is relatively temporally consistent if the maximum difference in their ages is less than the relative consistency threshold used by the application.
A deterministic workload model in which computations repeated at regular intervals provide a system function, e.g. digital control and constant bit-rate voice/video transmission.
A time interval of length H equal to the least common multiple of the periods pi of all periodic tasks in the system.
Fraction of time a truly periodic task with period pi and execution time ei keeps a processor busy, summed over all tasks.
Instant at which a job becomes available for execution; when the exact value is unknown, its range is called jitter.
A task whose jobs are released at random time instants but have hard deadlines; treated as a hard real-time task.
Constraints on the order in which jobs can execute arising from data and control dependencies; jobs that may execute in any order are said to be independent.
A valid schedule in which every job completes by its deadline and, in general, meets all its timing constraints.
The sum of the miss rate and the loss rate — the percentage of jobs that do not produce a useful result; schedulers seek to minimise it.
Scheduling in which decisions on which jobs execute when are made at specific time instants; the schedule is computed off-line and stored, minimising run-time overhead.
A round-robin variant that gives different jobs different weights, i.e. fractions of processor time per round; mainly used for real-time traffic in high-speed switched networks.
A class of event-driven, greedy scheduling algorithms that never leave a resource idle intentionally while some job needing it is ready; also called list or work-conserving scheduling.
A priority assignment whereby the earlier the deadline, the higher the priority; optimal for preemptable jobs on one processor with no resource contention.
The time by which a job with deadline d can afford to be delayed: the deadline minus time t minus remaining execution time.
An algorithm that assigns higher priority to jobs with smaller slack; also called Minimum-Laxity-First, it is optimal for preemptive jobs on one processor.
Unexpected timing behaviour of a priority-driven system in which shorter execution times, fewer dependencies or more processors can make jobs complete later.
The situation in which a lower-priority job runs in preference to a higher-priority job that has to wait.
A small non-negative integer returned by open() identifying an open file; fd = −1 indicates an error.
A UNIX file type used for inter-process communication between processes.
Data about file data — size, type, permissions, timestamps — maintained per file by the kernel and accessed by users with the stat and fstat functions.
A read/write that transfers fewer bytes than requested; it can occur on EOF, terminal reads, sockets and pipes, but never on disk-file reads and writes (other than EOF).
Set of buffered input-output wrappers that handle short counts efficiently in network programs and remain thread-safe.
Shell feature, such as ls > foo.txt, implemented by calling dup2(oldfd, newfd), which copies descriptor-table entry oldfd to entry newfd.
